title: Why Is a Software Glitch Called a Bug?
sources: Smithsonian National Museum of American History, 'Log Book With Computer Bug' (americanhistory.si.edu/collections/object/nmah_334663): on 9 Sept 1947 operators of the Harvard Mark II found a moth in Relay #70, Panel F, taped it into the log with the note 'First actual case of bug being found'

Wikipedia 'Bug (engineering)' and computinghistory.org.uk 'First computer bug is found': the moth was taped into the Mark II logbook at Harvard in 1947; the term 'bug' for a technical fault was already in use

Thomas Edison Papers, Rutgers (edisondigital.rutgers.edu), letters to Theodore Puskas, 1878, and Atlas Obscura 'Did Thomas Edison coin the term bug?': Edison described faults in his inventions as 'bugs' in 1878
General definition: a software bug is an error in code that makes a program behave differently from what was intended (e.g. a duplicate-charge bug)

lines.text: Why do we call a software glitch a bug?
lines.caps: WHY DO WE *CALL | A SOFTWARE *GLITCH | A *BUG?

lines.text: Well, a bug is when code does what you typed,
lines.caps: WELL, A *BUG | IS WHEN *CODE | DOES WHAT YOU *TYPED

lines.text: Like a shopping cart that charges you twice,
because one tiny line was off.
But the name has a wild story.
In nineteen forty seven, engineers at Harvard
found a real moth stuck inside their giant computer.
They taped it into the logbook with a little joke:
lines.caps: THEY *TAPED IT | INTO THE *LOGBOOK | WITH A LITTLE *JOKE

lines.text: first actual case of bug being found.
Thomas Edison was already calling glitches bugs
So the moth didn't invent the bug,
it just became the most famous one.
